questions.q: What is a chemical equation and what do its two sides show?
questions.a: A chemical equation states a reaction in symbols: the starting substances (reactants) sit on the left of an arrow and the new substances (products) on the right.

questions.q: Where are the reactants and products placed in a written chemical equation?
questions.a: Reactants are written on the left-hand side and products on the right-hand side, with an arrow between them pointing from reactants to products.

questions.q: Write the word equation for burning of magnesium ribbon in air.
questions.a: Magnesium + Oxygen -> Magnesium oxide (on burning, magnesium combines with oxygen of air to form white magnesium oxide).

questions.q: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
questions.a: Because mass is conserved in a reaction: atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so each element must have the same number of atoms on both sides.

questions.q: What is meant by a skeletal equation?
questions.a: A skeletal equation is an unbalanced equation that shows the formulas of reactants and products but not the equal atom counts on the two sides.

questions.q: How do you check whether an equation is balanced?
questions.a: Count the atoms of every element on the reactant side and on the product side; the equation is balanced only when each count matches, using smallest whole-number coefficients.

questions.q: What is a combination reaction? Give one example.
questions.a: Two or more substances join to form a single product, e.g. calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, or hydrogen and oxygen form water.

questions.q: How is a combination reaction different from a decomposition reaction?
questions.a: In combination many reactants give one product; in decomposition one reactant splits into two or more products - the two are opposites.

questions.q: Is burning of coal a combination reaction? Why?
questions.a: Yes; carbon of coal combines with oxygen of air to form a single product, carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What is an exothermic reaction?
questions.a: A reaction in which heat is released along with the products, making the surroundings warm.

questions.q: Give two everyday examples of exothermic reactions.
questions.a: Burning of natural gas (cooking) and respiration in cells; both release heat energy. Quicklime slaking with water is another.

questions.q: Why is decomposition of calcium carbonate in a lime kiln not exothermic?
questions.a: It needs continuous heat to proceed, so it is endothermic - energy is absorbed rather than released.

questions.q: What happens in a decomposition reaction?
questions.a: A single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances on heating, on light, or by electricity.

questions.q: Which type of energy can bring about decomposition? Give one example of each.
questions.a: Heat (ferrous sulphate gives ferric oxide, SO2 and SO3), light (silver chloride turns grey giving silver), and electricity (electrolysis of water gives hydrogen and oxygen).

questions.q: What is a photolytic decomposition? Name one white salt that behaves so.
questions.a: Decomposition driven by light; white silver chloride turns grey in sunlight, splitting into silver and chlorine.

questions.q: What is a displacement reaction?
questions.a: A more reactive element pushes out a less reactive element from its compound, e.g. iron nails dipped in copper sulphate solution take the copper's place.

questions.q: Why does iron displace copper from copper sulphate solution?
questions.a: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so iron atoms lose electrons more readily and push copper out of its salt solution.

questions.q: What is observed when an iron nail is kept in copper sulphate solution?
questions.a: The blue colour of the solution fades to greenish and a brownish deposit of copper collects on the nail.

questions.q: What is a double displacement reaction?
questions.a: Two compounds in solution swap their ions to form two new compounds, usually when an insoluble product (precipitate) or water forms.

questions.q: What is a precipitation reaction?
questions.a: A double displacement reaction in which an insoluble solid separates out, e.g. mixing sodium sulphate with barium chloride gives a white barium sulphate precipitate.

questions.q: Give one example where double displacement produces water.
questions.a: Acid-base neutralisation: sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid exchange ions to give sodium chloride and water.

questions.q: Which reactions are called precipitation reactions and why are they useful?
questions.a: Double displacement reactions that form an insoluble salt; they help identify ions in solution and prepare insoluble salts.

questions.q: What is the white precipitate when barium chloride meets sodium sulphate?
questions.a: Barium sulphate, an insoluble white solid, while sodium chloride stays dissolved.

questions.q: How can you tell from the solubility that a reaction will give a precipitate?
questions.a: If the product salt is insoluble in water while the reactant salts are soluble, an insoluble solid separates as a precipitate.

questions.q: What are oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen and hydrogen?
questions.a: Oxidation is gain of oxygen (or loss of hydrogen); reduction is loss of oxygen (or gain of hydrogen).

questions.q: What is a redox reaction?
questions.a: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction go on together: one substance loses oxygen/electrons while the other gains them.

questions.q: In the reaction of copper oxide with hydrogen, which substance is oxidised?
questions.a: Hydrogen is oxidised (it gains oxygen to become water) while copper oxide is reduced to copper.

questions.q: What is corrosion? Give two examples.
questions.a: Slow eating away of a metal by air and moisture; rusting of iron and green coating on copper are common examples.

questions.q: Why does silver turn black and copper turn green in air?
questions.a: Silver reacts with sulphur compounds of air to form black silver sulphide; copper forms a green basic carbonate with moist air.

questions.q: Name two methods to prevent corrosion.
questions.a: Painting or oiling the metal surface to keep off air and moisture, and galvanising iron with a zinc coat.

questions.q: What is rancidity?
questions.a: Oxidation of fats and oils in food on standing in air, which gives an unpleasant smell and taste.

questions.q: How can rancidity of fried food be prevented?
questions.a: By flushing packets with nitrogen, keeping food in airtight containers, refrigeration, and adding antioxidants.

questions.q: Why are chips packets flushed with nitrogen gas?
questions.a: Nitrogen is unreactive; it replaces oxygen so the oil in chips cannot oxidise and turn rancid.
